blocks.title: Ask Before Annotating
blocks.text: Never add a lifetime to make an error go away. First answer: which data does this output actually point into? The annotation then writes itself, or you learn the answer is "nothing" and you should return owned.

blocks.title: Signature Shorthand
items: `fn parse(s: &str) -> Parser<'_>` — borrowing, region unnamed.
`'_` in an `impl` header means "infer this one".
Prefer `'_` over an invented name you never reuse.
Passing `r: &mut T` to `fn f(x: &mut T)` reborrows `*r`.
So `r` is still usable after the call, despite not being `Copy`.
Write `&mut *r` explicitly when the target type is generic.
Otherwise inference moves the reference and you lose it.
`let a = &mut s.x; let b = &mut s.y;` — disjoint fields, allowed.
Through a method it fails: `fn get_x(&mut self)` borrows all of self.
Inline the field access instead of routing via an accessor.
`v.split_at_mut(mid)` yields two non-overlapping `&mut [T]`.

blocks.title: Why split_at_mut Needs unsafe
blocks.text: The checker cannot prove two index ranges are disjoint, so the standard library proves it by hand and hands you a safe signature. That is the pattern: unsafe inside, sound API outside.

caption.text: Part 3 of RUST BORROWING & LIFETIMES. The borrow checker is not fighting you — it is asking one question you have not answered: which region of code must this reference stay valid for? 10 pages of dense field notes: shared vs mutable borrows, NLL and two-phase borrows, lifetime elision in three rules, reborrows and splitting, interior mutability costs, and every borrow error code with the fix that actually works. Save it for the next time rustc prints three line numbers at you.
